Children begin by loving their parents; as they grow older they judge them; sometimes they forgive them.

What people call a soulmate is only the sexual instinct wearing a philosophical mask; once desire is satisfied, the mask quietly slips away, leaving two strangers staring at each other.
Sibling love conceals the oldest jealousy: we love our brothers and sisters, yet spend our lives never quite forgiving them for taking a share of the parental love that should have been wholly ours.
Wealth is like sea water; the more we drink, the thirstier we become; and the same is true of fame.
Life is a knot of desires; unfulfilled, they bring suffering, fulfilled, they bring boredom — and so life swings like a pendulum back and forth between pain and boredom.

Whatsoever is the object of any man's desire, that it is which he calls good; and the object of his hate, evil — for these words are never used with any constant signification, but always relative to the person that uses them.
Whoever desires necessarily desires that which he does not presently possess, that which is absent; the ontological essence of desire, then, is a directedness toward lack.
People's envy shows how unhappy they feel; their constant attention to the doings of others shows how bored they are.
Each class envies and emulates the class next above it in the social scale, while it rarely compares itself with those below or with those who are considerably in advance of itself.

Our standard of decency in expenditure, as in other ends of emulation, is set by the usage of those next above us in reputability; until, by insensible gradations, all canons of reputability and decency trace back to the usages and habits of thought of the wealthy leisure class.
It is never desire itself that torments us, but the gap between what we desire and what we are capable of.
What we long for is not wealth itself so much as the notice and approval it draws from others.
All of humanity's problems stem from man's inability to sit quietly in a room alone.
Kings and philosophers shit, and so do ladies. Even on the highest throne in the world, we are still sitting on our own arses.

Parents who expect gratitude from their children (there are even those who demand it) are like usurers who are happy to risk the capital as long as they get the interest.

The 'they', which is nothing definite, and which all are, though not as the sum, prescribes the kind of Being of everydayness.
The aspects of things that are most important for us are hidden because of their simplicity and familiarity. (One is unable to notice something — because it is always before one's eyes.)

Custom, then, is the great guide of human life. It is that principle alone which renders our experience useful to us, and makes us expect, for the future, a similar train of events with those which have appeared in the past. Without the influence of custom, we should be entirely ignorant of every matter of fact beyond what is immediately present to the memory and senses.

Even the most beautiful scenery is no longer assured of our love after we have lived in it for three months, and some distant coast attracts our avarice: possessions are generally diminished by possession.

The nitrogen in our DNA, the calcium in our teeth, the iron in our blood, the carbon in our apple pies were made in the interiors of collapsing stars. We are made of starstuff.

Voyager 1 launched in 1977, has traveled for about 50 years, and has covered roughly 25.9 billion kilometers — the farthest any human-made object has ever gone. And yet, at its current speed, reaching Proxima Centauri, our nearest star, 4 light-years away, would take about 70,000 years; leaving the galaxy at this speed would take billions of years. The cruelest truth of the universe is that it lets you look up at the stars, yet never lets you reach them.

One of the oldest and most enduring lies humanity has ever told itself is that nature contains purpose and order — the universe is indifferent to our existence, indifferent almost to the point of cruelty.
Nothing in nature is contingent, but all things are conditioned to exist and operate in a particular manner by the necessity of the divine nature.
What then is truth? A mobile army of metaphors, metonyms, anthropomorphisms — truths which are illusions about which one has forgotten that this is what they are.
Nature never lies; she is always sincere. It is we who are false, and who deceive ourselves and are deceived.

We have no other notion of cause and effect, but that of certain objects, which have been always conjoined together. We are determined by custom alone to expect the one from the appearance of the other.

Successive transition from one paradigm to another via revolution is the usual developmental pattern of mature science. The proponents of competing paradigms practice their trades in different worlds.

Human reason has this peculiar fate that in one species of its knowledge it is burdened by questions which, as prescribed by the very nature of reason itself, it is not able to ignore, but which, as transcending all its powers, it is also not able to answer.
The world is my representation — this is a truth valid with reference to every living and knowing being, although man alone can bring it into reflective and abstract consciousness.

If the sufferings of children go to make up the sum of sufferings which was necessary to pay for truth, then I protest that the truth is not worth such a price... I don't want harmony. I don't want it, out of love for humanity.
The passions that most of all cause the differences of wit are principally the more or less desire of power, of riches, of knowledge, and of honour.
Men are so simple, and so subject to present necessities, that he who seeks to deceive will always find someone who will allow himself to be deceived.
'Tis not contrary to reason to prefer the destruction of the whole world to the scratching of my finger.
So that in the first place, I put for a general inclination of all mankind, a perpetual and restless desire of power after power, that ceaseth only in death.

Men in general judge more by the eyes than by the hands, for everyone can see, but few can touch. Everyone sees what you appear to be, few really know what you are... of the nature of the people, it is easier to deceive them than to undeceive them.
Reason is perfectly inert, and can never either prevent or produce any action or affection.
Men believe themselves to be free, simply because they are conscious of their actions, and unconscious of the causes whereby those actions are determined.
A man who wishes to make a profession of goodness in everything must necessarily come to ruin among so many who are not good.
Where there is no common power, there is no law: where no law, no injustice. Force, and fraud, are in war the two cardinal virtues.
I judge indeed that it is true that fortune is the arbiter of one half of our actions, but that she still leaves us to direct the other half, or perhaps a little less.
The wheel of fortune turns round incessantly, and today's topmost is tomorrow's lowest.
Of things some are in our power, and others are not; opinions, desires, and aversions are in our power, but the body, property, reputation, and offices are not.
Fortune is like a raging river, but men can build dikes and dams to contain it before it floods.
Whatever comes by chance is unstable, and the higher it rises, the nearer it is to falling.
As thus she turns her wheel of chance with haughty hand, and presses on.
Do not seek for things to happen as you wish, but wish the things that happen to be as they are, and you will have a tranquil flow of life.
Whatever fortune has given to a man, she can take away, and what she gives comes with no covenant attached.
No man can ever be secure until he has been forsaken by Fortune.
All fortune is good fortune; for it either rewards, disciplines, amends, or punishes, and so is either useful or just.

Even when unable to know for certain which road is best, one should choose one direction firmly and follow it, as a traveler lost in a forest should never stand still.

The real choice a person must make in a lifetime is not among the countless possibilities the world offers, but whether they have the courage to become who they already are; most hesitation is really a refusal to face this simplest and cruelest answer.
Prudence is a true and reasoned capacity to act with regard to the things that are good for a human being.
Marry, and you will regret it; do not marry, you will also regret it; whichever you choose, you will regret both, for regret is the basic structure of human existence.
I see it all perfectly; there are two possible situations—one can either do this or that. My honest opinion and my friendly advice is this: do it or do not do it—you will regret both.

A truly profound mind should dare to suspend judgment for a long time, tolerating being torn between two opposing possibilities, rather than rushing into a hasty decision merely to buy the appearance of peace.

A truly independent spirit is bound to pass through a dangerous turning point—the moment when one must shatter with one's own hands the values one has always relied on, no longer asking any outside authority for the answer; this solitude of self-legislation is far heavier than freedom appears to be, and few ever truly dare to bear it.

To be troubled by another man's abuse is to grant him the right to judge you — and that alone is already a kind of self-diminishment.
Anger is a brief madness — what it craves is never self-mastery, but the ruin of others together with itself.
If you are told that a certain person speaks ill of you, do not make excuses about what is said of you, but answer: he was ignorant of my other faults, else he would not have mentioned these alone.

The greatest cure for anger is delay — ask this from anger at the start, not so it will forgive, but so it will judge rightly.

The cause of anger is the belief that we are injured; this belief should not be lightly entertained. We ought not to fly into a rage even when the injury appears open and distinct, for some false things bear the semblance of truth, and time discloses it.

Whoever attaches a lot of value to the opinions of others pays them too much honor.

I never can catch myself at any time without a perception, and never can observe any thing but the perception.

As far as this consciousness can be extended backwards to any past action or thought, so far reaches the identity of that person; it is the same self now as it was then; and it is by the same self with this present one that now reflects on it, that that action was done.

I may venture to affirm of the rest of mankind, that they are nothing but a bundle or collection of different perceptions, which succeed each other with an inconceivable rapidity, and are in a perpetual flux and movement.

On going inside, we should only see parts which push one another, and never anything by which to explain a perception.
The really hard problem of consciousness is the problem of experience. When we think and perceive, there is a whir of information-processing, but there is also a subjective aspect.

Would you not want this once more and innumerable times more?'
He who has learned how to die has unlearned how to be a slave; to philosophize is to learn how to die, and only then does a man rise each morning truly free.

Good sense is, of all things among men, the most equally distributed; for every one thinks himself so abundantly provided with it that even those who are the most difficult to satisfy in everything else do not usually desire more of this quality than they already possess.
A wise man proportions his belief to the evidence.
Thoughts without content are empty, intuitions without concepts are blind.
All men by nature desire to know.
The limits of my language mean the limits of my world.
If a lion could talk, we could not understand him.

Thus it happens that human knowledge, as we have it, is a mere medley and ill-digested mass, made up of much credulity and much accident, and also of the childish notions which we at first imbibed.
Faith consists in believing not what seems true, but what seems false to our understanding.

In philosophy, a student ought to doubt of the things he fancies he understands too easily, as much as of those he does not understand at all.

This immaturity is self-incurred if its cause is not lack of understanding, but lack of resolution and courage to use it without the guidance of another.
Laziness and cowardice are the reasons why such a large portion of men remain immature for life.
The whole problem with the world is that fools and fanatics are always so certain of themselves, and wiser people so full of doubts.
Man is by nature a political animal, and he who is unable to live in society is a beast or a god.—Man is not born fit for civil society, but is made fit for it by education.
Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains.—Before the establishment of civil society, mankind existed in a state of war of all against all.

The history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles.—The people never give up their liberties but under some delusion.

Because thought is free, every man remains at liberty to judge for himself whether a reputed miracle is worthy of belief, weighing what advantage those who claim or support it stand to gain, and thereby to judge whether the matter be a true wonder or an imposture.

It is much safer to be feared than loved, when one of the two must be lacking.—Yet a peace maintained by fear alone is nothing but unexploded hostility; a security never granted the reason and consent of one's subjects will in the end be destroyed by the very resentment that fear has stored up.

Dictatorship is the exercise of state power with the suspension of the legal restraints otherwise in force, in order to meet a state of emergency.—The state of emergency has always been the pretext by which the guarantees of individual liberty are eroded.

A state is a human community that successfully claims the monopoly of the legitimate use of physical force within a given territory.—War is a necessary instrument of the state, and peace is often little more than preparation for the next war.
The greatest danger in a democracy is not tyranny, but the tyranny of the majority, the oppression of the minority in the name of freedom.
War is nothing but the continuation of policy by other means, and thus the justice of a war cannot be judged apart from the political end it serves.

Evil comes not from fanaticism or perversion, but from banality—the most terrifying thing about totalitarian domination is that it seeks to destroy man's capacity for independent thought and judgment.

Even where societies begin from different premises, so long as they follow a set of reasonable basic rules, liberal societies and non-liberal but decent societies can still coexist and cooperate on a footing of mutual respect.

Justice is the first virtue of social institutions, as truth is of systems of thought; a theory however elegant must be rejected if untrue, and laws however efficient must be reformed if unjust.—Justice, in the end, is nothing but a refinement of the feeling of revenge.
